resistor-color-code-calculator.metaDescription: Free resistor color code calculator. Pick 4, 5 or 6 band colors to decode resistance, tolerance and ppm instantly — runs 100% in your browser.
resistor-color-code-calculator.keywords: resistor color code calculator, resistor decoder, 4 band resistor, 5 band resistor, resistance calculator
resistor-color-code-calculator.quickAnswer: Read the colored bands on a resistor from the end with the most bands: the first bands are digits, the next is the multiplier, then tolerance. For example, yellow-violet-red-gold is 47 × 100 = 4,700 Ω (4.7 kΩ) with ±5% tolerance.
keyFacts: Resistor color codes are an IEC standard: each color represents a digit, a multiplier, a tolerance, or a temperature coefficient.
4-band resistors have 2 digits + multiplier + tolerance; 5-band have 3 digits; 6-band adds a temperature coefficient (ppm/K).
Gold and silver appear only as multipliers (×0.1, ×0.01) or tolerance bands (±5%, ±10%) — never as digit bands.
A missing tolerance band means ±20%. That is the loosest common tolerance.
The tolerance tells you the guaranteed range: a 4.7 kΩ ±5% resistor is guaranteed between 4,465 Ω and 4,935 Ω.
ppm/K (parts per million per kelvin) on the 6th band tells how much resistance drifts with temperature — important for precision circuits.
howTo: Choose 4, 5, or 6 bands to match the bands printed on your resistor.
Tap the colored swatches for each band, in order from left to right as printed on the resistor body.
Read the nominal resistance, tolerance, and guaranteed min–max range in the results.
For 6-band resistors, also note the temperature coefficient (ppm/K).
Compare the measured value with a multimeter: it should fall inside the tolerance range.
resistor-color-code-calculator.formula:
R = (digit bands as a number) x multiplier
Min = R x (1 - tolerance/100), Max = R x (1 + tolerance/100)
resistor-color-code-calculator.workedExample:
A 4-band resistor shows yellow, violet, red, gold.
Digits: yellow = 4, violet = 7 → 47
Multiplier: red = x100 → 47 x 100 = 4,700 Ω = 4.7 kΩ
Tolerance: gold = ±5%
Range: 4,700 x 0.95 = 4,465 Ω to 4,700 x 1.05 = 4,935 Ω
So the resistor is 4.7 kΩ ±5% (4,465–4,935 Ω).
benefits: Decodes any standard 4, 5, or 6-band resistor in seconds — no chart memorization needed.
Shows the guaranteed min–max range, so you know what a multimeter should read.
Explains the 6th band (ppm/K) that confuses most beginners.
Works offline in your browser — handy on a workbench with no internet.
limitations: Covers standard IEC color codes only — not SMD numeric codes (like 472) or EIA-96 codes.
The colors you pick must match the resistor: faded or burnt bands can mislead, so verify with a multimeter for critical circuits.
Does not account for power rating (watts) — check the resistor's physical size or datasheet separately.
An educational decoder, not a substitute for measurement in precision work.

faqs.q: Which end do I read a resistor from?
faqs.a: Start from the end closest to the bands. The tolerance band (gold, silver, or others) is usually spaced slightly apart at the right end — start from the opposite end.

faqs.q: What do gold and silver bands mean?
faqs.a: As a multiplier, gold means ×0.1 and silver means ×0.01. As a tolerance band, gold means ±5% and silver means ±10%. They never represent digits.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 4-band and 5-band resistors?
faqs.a: 4-band resistors use 2 digit bands and are typical for E12/E24 series values. 5-band resistors add a third digit for finer E48/E96/E192 series values, common in precision parts.
It is the temperature coefficient in ppm/K — how many parts per million the resistance changes per degree kelvin. Lower is more stable; 50 ppm/K or less is typical for precision resistors.

faqs.q: My resistor has no tolerance band. What then?
faqs.a: A missing tolerance band means ±20% tolerance. Pick None for the tolerance band in this tool to get the correct range.

faqs.q: Can two bands have the same color?
faqs.a: Yes. Digit bands can repeat freely — for example brown-black-black is 10 Ω. Only the role of each position matters.
